source.title: Open problems of the 32nd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

accepted.question_text: Let G be a 3-connected cubic graph. Does every such graph admit a blue-red colouring of its vertices such that the blue vertices induce a subgraph B with maximum degree at most 1, the red vertices induce a subgraph R with minimum degree at least 1, and R satisfies some relaxation of the condition 'R contains no path with 3 edges'? In other words, which weakened structural condition on the red induced subgraph R is sufficient to guarantee the existence of a crumby-type colouring for every 3-connected cubic graph?

evidence.quote:
Problem 1.1 What relaxation of the conditions on R guarantees that such a coloring of
a 3-connected cubic graph always exists?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a graph G whose list packing number χ⋆ℓ(G) exceeds its list-chromatic number χℓ(G) by more than 1; that is, is there a graph with χ⋆ℓ(G) > χℓ(G) + 1? Here χℓ(G) is the least k such that every k-list-assignment of G has a proper colouring, and χ⋆ℓ(G) is the least k such that every k-list-assignment of G admits k pairwise disjoint proper list-colourings.

accepted.question_text: Is the list packing number of every graph at most twice its list-chromatic number? Equivalently, does χ⋆ℓ(G) ≤ 2χℓ(G) hold for every graph G, where χ⋆ℓ(G) denotes the minimum k such that every k-list-assignment admits k pairwise disjoint proper list-colourings?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a cubic planar graph and let L be a 3-list-assignment on V(G), meaning that each vertex receives a list of exactly three available colours. Must there always exist two proper L-colourings c1 and c2 that are disjoint at every vertex, i.e. c1(v) ≠ c2(v) for every v ∈ V(G)?
accepted.context_brief: Two disjoint list-colourings for cubic planar graphs

Problem 2.3 Is it possible to choose two disjoint proper colourings?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a cubic planar graph and let L be a 3-list-assignment on V(G). Must there always exist three proper L-colourings c1, c2, c3 that are pairwise disjoint at every vertex, meaning ci(v) ≠ cj(v) whenever i ≠ j and v ∈ V(G)?
accepted.context_brief: Three disjoint list-colourings for cubic planar graphs

evidence.quote: Problem 2.4 Is it possible to choose three disjoint proper colourings?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a cubic bipartite graph and let L be a 3-list-assignment on V(G). It is stated that two disjoint proper L-colourings can be found in this setting. Is it always possible to find three proper L-colourings that are pairwise disjoint at every vertex?
accepted.context_brief: Three disjoint list-colourings for cubic bipartite graphs

evidence.quote:
In the case of cubic bipartite graphs, it is possible to find two disjoint proper colourings
(problem similar to Problem 3) [unpublished]. Hence, the following question arises: Is it possible
to find three disjoint proper colourings in the case of cubic bipartite graphs?

accepted.question_text: Let n = 4k + 1 for some integer k ≥ 1, let S be a k-element subset of {1,2,…,2k}, and define the extended Petersen graph XP(2n,S) to have vertex set Z_n × {1,2} and edge set {x1y1 : d(x,y) ∈ S} ∪ {x2y2 : d(x,y) ∈ {1,…,2k} \ S} ∪ {x1x2 : x ∈ Z_n}, where d(x,y) = min{|x−y|, n−|x−y|}. Is every extended Petersen graph other than the Petersen graph itself a Class 1 graph, meaning that its chromatic index equals its maximum degree?

evidence.quote:
Conjecture 3.1 (Hor´ak, Rosa [1]) Every extended Petersen graph, except Petersen
graph itself, is of Class 1.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a constant c ≥ 0 such that every non-complete graph G of order n with minimum degree δ(G) ≥ n/2 + c has rainbow connection number rc(G) equal to 2? In particular, does the weaker condition δ(G) ≥ n/2 already imply rc(G) = 2? Here rc(G) is the minimum number of colours needed to edge-colour G so that every two vertices are joined by a path whose edges all have distinct colours.
accepted.context_brief: Rainbow connection under large minimum degree

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a 5-edge-connected 5-regular graph that is Class 2, that is, a 5-regular graph whose edges cannot be coloured with only 5 colours?

evidence.quote:
Problem 5.1 (Ma, Mattiolo, Steffen, Wolf [1]) Is there any 5-edge-connected 5-
regular Class 2 graph?

accepted.question_text: Is there a 5-edge-connected 5-graph that is poorly matchable? Here a 5-graph means a 5-regular graph G such that every odd vertex set X is joined to its complement by at least 5 edges, and 'poorly matchable' means that any two perfect matchings of G intersect.

evidence.quote:
An r-graph is an r-regular graph G such that every odd set X ⊆ V (G) is connected by at
least r edges to its complement V (G) \ X. An r-graph is poorly matchable if any two of its
perfect matchings intersect. ...
Problem 5.2 Is there a poorly matchable 5-edge-connected 5-graph?

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to characterize all subcubic triangle-free graphs of Class 2? Equivalently, can one describe exactly those graphs G with maximum degree at most 3, containing no triangle K3, whose chromatic index is 4 rather than Δ(G)?

evidence.quote: Problem 6.1 Is it possible to describe all subcubic K3-free graphs of Class 2?

accepted.question_text: Given a graph G, can one decide in polynomial time whether G has a Type-A order or a Type-B order of its vertices? A Type-A order is a linear order v1,…,vn in which every vertex v has an odd number of earlier neighbours or none; a Type-B order is a linear order in which every vertex either has an odd number of earlier neighbours or none, or else has an even number of earlier neighbours and no later neighbours.
accepted.context_brief: Recognition of Type-A and Type-B orders

evidence.quote:
Problem 7.1 Can it be decided in polynomial time whether a graph G admits a Type-A
order, or a Type-B order?

accepted.question_text: If a graph G admits a Type-A order or a Type-B order of its vertices, can such an order be found in polynomial time? Here a Type-A order is a linear order in which each vertex has an odd number of earlier neighbours or none, and a Type-B order is a linear order in which each vertex either satisfies the same condition or has an even number of earlier neighbours and no later neighbours.

evidence.quote: Problem 7.2 If a Type-A or Type-B order exists, can it be found in polynomial time?
